item.title: “It felt like being an astronaut”: Mapping the ice beneath Antarctica | Geo Week News
item.summary: Close GIS Open GIS . GIS . View All. Standards. Industry protocols and best ... “It felt like being an astronaut”: Mapping the ice beneath Antarctica.
item.page_text:
By Fabio Giannino, Global Product Training Manager, IDS GeoRadar and all images are credited to Matthieu Tordeur and Dr. Heïdi Sevestre.
Polar science projects have traditionally relied on tractors and snowmobiles that burn huge amounts of fuel, so research into climate change has itself carried an environmental cost. The approach has also left much of Antarctica unmapped, because collecting accurate radar data means contending with extreme cold, rough terrain and a landscape that offers no easy way in.
Yet scientists urgently need to understand how Antarctica is responding to climate change so they can better predict consequences like rising sea levels.
To look beneath the surface, a new approach was needed. With UNESCO for the Decade of Action for Cryospheric Sciences, glaciologist Dr Heïdi Sevestre and polar explorer Matthieu Tordeur crossed the continent with two ground-penetrating radars (GPR). Powered only by wind and solar energy, the pair completed the first radar transect by kite-ski for polar science.
The expedition delivered the first dataset from some of Antarctica’s most remote regions, and showed that polar science can be sustainable without compromising the data needed to understand changing ice levels and the environment.
The challenges of scanning a frozen continent
The set-up on the ice, including the GPR, provided by IDS GeoRadar, and a GNSS receiver from Leica Geosystems, in action despite freezing temperatures.
The team set out to map both ancient and recent ice layers, record snow accumulation, and harmonize existing data from the few regions that had already been mapped to create a single picture.
Achieving the goals of the expedition meant battling extreme cold. Temperatures dropped as low as -50°C, beyond anything a standard freezer reaches.
“The environment was the biggest challenge,” explains Dr Heïdi Sevestre, “It’s a different planet, a different universe. The biting cold can suck the energy out of everything, especially the batteries. Each night, we slept with the batteries in our sleeping bags to keep them warm.
We were also battling unpredictable winds. It was either too violent, or if the wind dropped and conditions were too calm, it was impossible to take off on our skis. This was a huge challenge because the speed of travel is really important. Moving too fast or too slow can compromise the quality of the radar measurements.”
Adding to this, Antarctica’s terrain is made up of metre-high ice dunes, which made skiing difficult; the team had to tow around 200 kg of equipment across the bumpy surface.
All this left little room for error. With so much attention focused on survival and avoiding falls and frostbite, the time available for research was precious. Success depended on careful planning and the right technology that could survive the conditions and deliver accurate data.
Mapping Antarctica using kites, skis and ground penetrating radar
To tackle the wind and the cold, the team used the complex conditions to their advantage. Kite skiing offered a way to tow the radar on sleds with no fuel and no generator.
“We used kites of different sizes for different wind speeds to help us travel,” explains Sevestre. “You don’t want to be skiing too fast, so it was the best way to collect the data. Even when a kite was punctured and had holes, it was still repairable.”
The radar had to be just as resilient. “Ground-penetrating radar is usually used for utility detection, but the compact surface system turned out to be robust and perfect for icy conditions,” says Sevestre. “It works a bit like sonar, scanning whatever is beneath your feet. We used a shallow radar to scan the upper 40 metres of the Antarctic ice sheet. Almost everything broke during our journey but the radar. It remained reliable from start to finish, and that’s what let us capture the data we came for.”
The contents towed on the sled: the Chaser XR GPR, Leica GS16 GNSS receiver and Panasonic FZ-55 semi-rugged laptop.
Rather than the wheel-based trigger common in utility surveys, which would struggle on snow, measurements were triggered by GPS, with positioning from a GNSS receiver. The team used a surface shallow radar, which they checked every two hours for any faults or errors. A second radar worked alongside it to reveal deeper ice layers and map the bedrock, scanning up to two kilometers below the surface.
Over roughly 80 days and 4,000 kilometers of travel, both radars collected more than 1,500 kilometers of linear data, revealing for the first time what had previously been invisible beneath the ice.
From the ice to the inbox: processing the scanning data
When undertaking a project like this in a remote location, data is usually processed back in the office. But this was the first expedition in Antarctica with an internet connection, meaning the expedition team could store the data in the cloud and send it to the office in daily batches.
Back at the IDS GeoRadar office in Italy, each batch arrived in near real-time, where the team could monitor the equipment and troubleshoot remotely. Sevestre and Tordeur’s position was also updated in Google Earth every day.
“You can do science differently today,” says Sevestre. “It’s like being an astronaut with a Houston course-correcting you on the way. There’s a bigger team supporting us from miles away, and it felt comforting.”
Lenin’s bust at the Southern Pole of Inaccessibility, which fewer people have reached than the moon.
Some of the most valuable data came from the most remote places. After 42 days and nearly 1,800 kilometers of kite-skiing, Sevestre and Tordeur arrived at the Southern Pole of Inaccessibility, historically calculated as the point in Antarctica farthest from any coastline. A bust of Lenin still overlooks a Soviet scientific base built in 1958, now buried beneath the snow.

item.title: Drones help archaeologists find Aboriginal rock art sites hidden in Australia's rugged Blue Mountains
item.summary: ... LiDAR (light detection and ranging) to identify three previously unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters containing rock art and stone artifacts. LiDAR ...
item.page_text:
edited by Swati Mestri , 																								reviewed by Robert Egan
This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted
														the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:
Drone-mounted laser technology is helping archaeologists locate Aboriginal rock art sites hidden in the rugged, densely vegetated landscapes of Australia's Blue Mountains, demonstrating a new approach to surveying archaeological sites that can be difficult and expensive to reach on foot.
Researchers from the University of Sydney and the Australian Museum, working alongside the Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation, used drone-based LiDAR (light detection and ranging) to identify three previously unregistered Aboriginal rock shelters containing rock art and stone artifacts.
LiDAR (light detection and ranging) uses laser pulses to create detailed 3D maps of the landscape, helping researchers detect features hidden beneath dense vegetation and tree cover. The newly recorded shelters contain visually striking rock art, including red hand stencils, as well as stone artifacts.
The team says the approach could help Aboriginal communities, archaeologists and heritage managers locate and protect cultural sites more efficiently across Australia.
The research is published in Remote Sensing .
The work forms part of the Gulamada Project , which is built on the principle of walking side by side, bringing together scientific knowledge and First Nations cultural knowledge to better understand and care for Country.
"From the outset, our vision for the Gulamada Project has been to create a true nexus of science and culture. This work highlights the importance of listening, learning and working together," said project co-director and Indigenous rock art expert Wayne Brennan at the University of Sydney.
Susan Templeman, the federal member for Macquarie, which includes the Blue Mountains, said, "This project demonstrates the power of bringing together First Nations knowledge and new technology to better understand and protect Australia's rich cultural heritage. I'm proud that the Australian government's First Nations Heritage Grants program is supporting important projects like Gulamada here in the Blue Mountains, already renowned for the extraordinary natural and cultural significance within our rugged landscapes."
The drone-based field surveys confirmed the locations of six registered rock shelters and three previously unregistered shelters containing rock art and stone artifacts. The work also produced much more accurate coordinates than those listed in the official New South Wales sites register—the Aboriginal Heritage Information Management System (AHIMS).
After the drone surveys identified potential rock shelter sites, project co-director Dr. Amy Mosig Way, a research archaeologist at the University of Sydney and the Australian Museum, led teams of students and volunteers into the field to verify the locations and assess whether the shelters contained cultural material.
Brennan and Erin Wilkins (Dharug Custodian Aboriginal Corporation) then led the rock art recording at confirmed sites.
"One of the most rewarding aspects of the Gulamada Project has been creating opportunities for students to gain hands-on experience in cultural heritage research in a community-centered project," Way said.

More than 200 rock shelters containing cultural and archaeological evidence have been recorded in the Blue Mountains. Yet, according to Way, only an estimated 10% of the region has been surveyed because of its rugged and difficult terrain.
The new methodology enables Aboriginal communities, archaeologists and heritage managers to search vast areas of challenging landscape much faster than traditional ground surveys.
"This work is exciting because it offers an efficient and accurate way to locate sites in rugged environments, which are notoriously arduous, expensive and time-consuming to survey," said Dr. Jacob Bongers, lead author on the drone research and a digital archaeologist at the University of Sydney. He is also a former AMF/AMRI visiting research fellow at the Australian Museum.
"Importantly, our methodology is helping expand the record of Aboriginal cultural sites in the Blue Mountains and has the potential to be applied in other regions," Bongers said.
While identifying previously unregistered rock shelters is significant, the broader impact may be the ability to find and safeguard many more cultural sites across Australia using a faster and more targeted approach.
The technology provides Aboriginal communities with another tool to use alongside existing knowledge and cultural practices to locate, document and protect important heritage sites before they are affected by development, erosion, wildfires or other threats.
These promising results lay the groundwork for further LiDAR-assisted surveys across Australia in partnership with Aboriginal communities.
The research team plans to work with Aboriginal communities to test and adapt the approach in different environments, including the tropical savannas of western Arnhem Land and the semiarid landscapes of western New South Wales.
Ultimately, the methodology could become more than a tool for locating archaeological sites. It has the potential to support Aboriginal communities in documenting, managing and safeguarding cultural landscapes for future generations.
Jacob L. Bongers et al., LiDAR-Assisted Survey Locates Unregistered Rock Shelters in the Blue Mountains, Australia, Remote Sensing (2026). DOI: 10.3390/rs18203495

item.summary: The project integrates genomic data with terrestrial and UAV Lidar ... GNSS · Mobile Mapping · Point Clouds. General. Advertise · About us · Contact ...
item.page_text:
Carinthia University of Applied Sciences (CUAS) has equipped its new Interdisciplinary Center for Ecosystem Services and Biodiversity (ICEB) with terrestrial and UAV-based laser scanning systems from RIEGL. The investment establishes a combined TLS/ULS capability at the center, aimed at high-precision 3D data acquisition for biodiversity research and the quantitative assessment of ecosystem services.
The delivery comprises a RIEGL VZ-600i terrestrial laser scanner and a VUX-120-23 UAV laser scanning system, the latter integrated with a positioning unit and camera on a heavy-lift drone platform. The pairing allows the team to capture detailed stem and understory structure from the ground while covering canopy and larger survey areas from the air, producing complementary point clouds suited to forest structure analysis at both plot and landscape scale.
The equipment forms part of CUAS’s “BioDivTechLab” project, funded by the Austrian Research Promotion Agency (FFG) through its R&D infrastructure program and co-financed by the European Union. It reflects growing investment by Austrian research institutions in remote sensing infrastructure for environmental applications, where quantifying ecosystem services such as carbon storage and habitat structure is increasingly in demand.
One of the first projects to use the systems is an international study funded by the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), titled “Seeing the Forest for the Trees.” It investigates how genetic variation among individual trees influences the performance of beech forests. The project integrates genomic data with terrestrial and UAV Lidar forest monitoring and satellite remote sensing, covering more than 1,000 beech trees across Europe.
The consortium includes the Spatial Genetics of the Environment group at the University of Zurich’s Department of Geography, CUAS’s ICEB in Villach, the Department of Genetics at Kazimierz Wielki University in Bydgoszcz, Poland, and partners in Romania and Germany.
In early September, CUAS’s SIENA department (Spatial Informatics for Environmental Applications), led by Prof Gernot Paulus, visited the manufacturer’s headquarters in Horn for system handover, acceptance testing and in-depth training. SIENA is responsible for Lidar technologies within the newly founded ICEB.
